questions.question:
A financial services company stores compliance audit logs in Amazon S3 and must retain them immutably for 7 years to satisfy SEC 17a-4 regulations. The security architect must ensure that no user, including those with Administrator access or root credentials, can delete or shorten the retention period during that window.

Which S3 Object Lock configuration satisfies this requirement?

choices.text: Apply S3 Object Lock in Governance mode with a 7-year retention period and deny the `s3:BypassGovernanceRetention` action in all IAM policies.
choices.explanation: Governance mode has a loophole: users with `s3:BypassGovernanceRetention` permission can override it, and that includes root. You might think denying this in IAM policies would fix things, but IAM deny statements don't apply to the root account.

choices.text: Apply S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode with a 7-year retention period on the bucket.
choices.explanation: Compliance mode enforces true WORM (Write Once Read Many) immutability. Nobody can override it, not admins, not even root, for the entire retention period. It's the only Object Lock mode that actually meets strict regulatory requirements like SEC 17a-4.

choices.text: Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket and configure an S3 Lifecycle policy to expire objects after 7 years, combined with an S3 bucket policy that denies `s3:DeleteObject`.
choices.explanation: Versioning with a bucket policy stops casual deletions but doesn't enforce true immutability. A bucket owner can just modify or remove the policy whenever they want. Worse, Lifecycle expiration actively deletes objects, which is the exact opposite of what you need here.

choices.text: Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket, configure MFA Delete, and apply an SCP that denies `s3:PutBucketPolicy` changes for 7 years.
choices.explanation: MFA Delete adds protection for version deletions but doesn't create a fixed retention window. SCPs only govern member accounts in Organizations and can't stop the management account or root from changing policies. Therefore, this combination still falls short of what SEC 17a-4 requires.

questions.tip: You need a retention mode that absolutely nobody can override - not even root users. Which one locks down data permanently?
questions.explanation:
When you need true regulatory compliance, Compliance mode is your only option. Here's why: once you set it, nobody can change it - not administrators, not root users, nobody. The retention period is locked in stone.

The other approaches have escape hatches:
- Governance mode sounds similar but users with `s3:BypassGovernanceRetention` permission can override it, and root always has this capability regardless of IAM policies
- Versioning plus lifecycle policies can be changed by bucket owners at any time
- MFA Delete and SCPs add layers but don't create an immutable retention window

For SEC 17a-4 compliance, you need that iron-clad guarantee that Compliance mode provides.

questions.question:
A security team at a healthcare company suspects that CloudTrail log files stored in their centralized S3 bucket were deleted and recreated with modified content by a compromised administrator account. The team needs a native AWS mechanism that can cryptographically prove whether logs were altered after CloudTrail delivered them to S3.

Which feature provides this capability?

choices.text: CloudTrail log file validation, which generates hourly digest files containing SHA-256 hashes of all delivered log files, signed by AWS using a private key.
choices.explanation: Log file validation creates hourly digest files containing SHA-256 hashes of every log delivered in that window. AWS signs these digests with their RSA private key, so when you run `aws cloudtrail validate-logs` it recomputes the hashes and checks them against those signed digests, catching any modification, deletion or injection. It even detects cases where someone deleted and recreated the log files from scratch.

choices.text: Amazon Macie configured to scan the CloudTrail S3 bucket for sensitive data patterns and alert when log file sizes deviate from a baseline.
choices.explanation: Macie is built for sensitive data discovery and anomaly detection and doesn't provide cryptographic proof of file integrity. Size-based alerts are heuristic, so if someone modified the content without changing the file size, Macie wouldn't catch it.

choices.text: S3 Object Lock in Governance mode applied to the CloudTrail bucket, preventing modification of log files during the retention window.
choices.explanation: Governance mode prevents deletion during a retention period but can't retroactively verify whether files were tampered with after delivery. It also has no way to detect if a privileged user with `s3:BypassGovernanceRetention` swapped out files before the lock kicked in.

choices.text: AWS Config rule cloudtrail-s3-dataevents-enabled to monitor whether the CloudTrail bucket receives new objects, triggering an SNS alert on anomalies.
choices.explanation: Config managed rules check whether your setup matches compliance standards and can't do cryptographic verification of log file content. This particular rule only checks if data events are enabled, so it tells you nothing about whether delivered logs are genuine or have been tampered with.

questions.tip: You're looking for something that can prove a file hasn't been tampered with after it was created. What AWS feature gives you cryptographic proof?
questions.explanation:
Here's the key insight: you need cryptographic proof that files haven't been messed with after delivery. CloudTrail log file validation is the only option that actually does this.

What makes this work? AWS creates hourly SHA-256 digest files and signs them with their RSA private key. When you run `aws cloudtrail validate-logs`, it recomputes the hashes and checks them against those signed digests. If someone modified, deleted, or added files after delivery, you'll know immediately.

The other options miss the mark:
- Macie is great for finding sensitive data, but it doesn't verify file integrity
- Object Lock Governance mode stops future changes but can't tell you about past tampering (plus it can be bypassed anyway)
- Config rules check if your setup matches policies, not whether files have been altered

To enable this: use `--enable-log-file-validation` when creating your trail, or add it to an existing one.

questions.question:
A media company stores master video assets in S3 and requires that accidental overwrites by developers preserve the previous object content and that permanent deletion of any specific version requires multi-factor authentication from the bucket owner. The solution must use native S3 capabilities without restricting the development team's ability to upload new versions.

Which TWO configurations should the security engineer apply?

choices.text: Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket so that all PUT operations create a new version rather than overwriting the existing object.
choices.explanation: Versioning turns every overwrite into a new object version instead of replacing what's already there. Developers keep full write access and all original content stays recoverable. Delete operations just add a delete marker and previous versions remain untouched.

choices.text: Enable MFA Delete on the versioned bucket, requiring the bucket owner to supply a valid MFA code when permanently deleting a specific object version or suspending versioning.
choices.explanation: MFA Delete puts the most destructive S3 operations behind a hardware MFA token that only the bucket owner can provide. Both permanent version deletion and versioning suspension require that MFA code, so no developer or compromised credential can permanently wipe out object history without it.

choices.text: Apply S3 Object Lock in Governance mode with a 90-day retention period and grant all developers the `s3:BypassGovernanceRetention` permission for operational flexibility.
choices.explanation: Granting `s3:BypassGovernanceRetention` to every developer completely defeats the purpose of Object Lock. On top of that, the fixed retention period would stop developers from correcting accidental uploads, which directly conflicts with their operational needs.

choices.text: Configure an S3 bucket policy that denies `s3:DeleteObject` for all IAM principals except the bucket owner, and enable S3 Versioning.
choices.explanation: Denying `s3:DeleteObject` via bucket policy blocks deletion of the current object but misses the real target. With versioning enabled, permanent removal requires `s3:DeleteObjectVersion`, which is a completely different action. The policy also doesn't enforce MFA, and the bucket owner can change it whenever they want.

choices.text: Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication with delete marker replication disabled and rely on the replica bucket as the authoritative copy for recovery.
choices.explanation: CRR copies objects to another region for availability but doesn't stop permanent deletion in the source bucket. Turning off delete marker replication causes the replica to gradually drift out of sync with the source. Neither approach adds MFA enforcement to delete operations.

questions.tip: Think of this as two separate problems: keeping previous versions when files get overwritten, and requiring extra authorization before anything gets permanently deleted.
questions.explanation:
These two features solve different problems. Versioning keeps every object version around so developers can recover anything they accidentally overwrite. MFA Delete locks down the destructive stuff: permanently deleting a version or suspending versioning both require a hardware MFA code from the bucket owner.

**Why the other options fall short:**
- Giving every developer `s3:BypassGovernanceRetention` permission completely undermines Object Lock protection.
- A bucket policy denying `s3:DeleteObject` targets the wrong action. With versioning on, you need to block `s3:DeleteObjectVersion` instead and there's no MFA enforcement either.
- Cross-Region Replication provides availability in another region but nothing to prevent deletion at the source.

**To set this up:** `aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket <bucket-name> --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled,MFADelete=Enabled --mfa "<serial-number> <token-code>"` (must be run as the root account).

questions.question:
A compliance engineer must lock a Glacier vault's access policy to enforce a 10-year retention requirement for archived medical records. The vault and an InProgress vault lock policy have already been created. The engineer must complete the lock using the AWS CLI and only has the lock ID from the `initiate-vault-lock` response.

Which command correctly completes the vault lock?

choices.text:
aws glacier complete-vault-lock \
  --account-id - \
  --vault-name medical-records-vault \
  --lock-id <lockId>
choices.explanation: `complete-vault-lock` moves the vault lock from InProgress to the permanent Locked state using the lock ID you got from `initiate-vault-lock`. The `--account-id -` flag tells the CLI to use your current account. Once locked, the policy becomes truly immutable and nobody can delete or modify it.

choices.text:
aws glacier set-vault-access-policy \
  --account-id - \
  --vault-name medical-records-vault \
  --policy file://lock-policy.json
choices.explanation: `set-vault-access-policy` manages the standard (mutable) access policy on a vault and has nothing to do with the vault lock mechanism. It won't transition your InProgress lock to the Locked state, and policies set this way can be changed at any time. Not what you need for compliance.

choices.text:
aws glacier initiate-vault-lock \
  --account-id - \
  --vault-name medical-records-vault \
  --policy file://lock-policy.json
choices.explanation: `initiate-vault-lock` starts a new InProgress vault lock, but you've already done that step. Running it again would abort your existing InProgress policy and restart the 24-hour completion window from scratch, which is the opposite of what you want.

choices.text:
aws glacier put-vault-lock \
  --account-id - \
  --vault-name medical-records-vault \
  --lock-id <lockId>
choices.explanation: `put-vault-lock` doesn't exist in the Glacier CLI. The correct two-step process goes `initiate-vault-lock` (creates the InProgress policy and gives you a lock ID) then `complete-vault-lock` (finalizes it permanently). Running a nonexistent subcommand just returns an error.

questions.tip: Glacier Vault Lock is a two-phase process: you start it then finalize it. Which phase makes the lock permanent?
questions.explanation:
Glacier Vault Lock works in two phases. First, `initiate-vault-lock` creates an InProgress policy and hands you a lock ID, kicking off a 24-hour window to test everything. Then `complete-vault-lock` uses that lock ID to make the policy permanent.

**Why the other commands don't work:**
- `set-vault-access-policy` manages regular mutable access policies. It has nothing to do with the vault lock mechanism.
- Running `initiate-vault-lock` again would abort your existing InProgress lock and reset the 24-hour timer back to zero.
- `put-vault-lock` simply doesn't exist in the Glacier API.

**To complete the lock:** `aws glacier complete-vault-lock --account-id - --vault-name <vault-name> --lock-id <lockId>` (the `--account-id -` flag is required by the Glacier CLI).

questions.question: A security architect is documenting the data integrity controls for a multi-tier compliance platform on AWS. Each control addresses a distinct data integrity scenario. Match each integrity requirement to the AWS mechanism that best satisfies it.

slots.label: Detect tampering of audit log files after delivery to S3
Prevent any user from deleting archived records for a fixed regulatory period
Ensure software releases have not been altered since the publisher signed them
Preserve all previous object states when developers overwrite S3 objects

choices.text: CloudTrail log file validation with SHA-256 digest files
choices.explanation: CloudTrail log file validation generates hourly SHA-256 digest files that AWS signs with their RSA private key. Running `aws cloudtrail validate-logs` recomputes the hashes and checks them against those signed digests, so you'll immediately know if any log was modified, deleted, or injected after delivery.

choices.text: S3 Versioning to convert overwrites into new object versions
choices.explanation: S3 Versioning keeps every object version by turning PUT operations into new versions instead of replacements. DELETE operations become recoverable delete markers. You can restore any prior state just by referencing its version ID.

choices.text: S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode with a fixed retention period
choices.explanation: Compliance mode enforces WORM immutability that nobody, including root, can override during the retention window. This is the go-to control for regulatory archive requirements like SEC 17a-4 or HIPAA retention mandates.

choices.text: Digital code signing verified against a trusted certificate authority
choices.explanation: Digital code signing uses asymmetric cryptography: a publisher signs a release with their private key and any recipient can verify the signature against the corresponding public certificate. If the signature doesn't match, you know the software was tampered with or corrupted after signing.

questions.tip: Each control protects data in a different way: some prevent changes, others detect tampering after the fact and some preserve history. Match the protection style to the threat.
questions.explanation:
Think of data integrity as layers, each covering a different scenario.

CloudTrail log file validation catches tampering after the fact. It uses cryptographically signed digests to prove whether audit logs have been modified since delivery.

S3 Object Lock Compliance mode is your regulatory compliance tool. Once enabled, nobody (not even root) can delete or modify objects during the retention period. It's immutable storage that satisfies the strictest archive requirements.

Digital code signing proves software authenticity. It's how you verify that a release actually came from the legitimate publisher and hasn't been altered along the way.

S3 Versioning is your safety net for human error. Every time someone overwrites a file, the previous version sticks around so you can recover it later.
